summary: Describes principles of traffic engineering in IP networks and gives a common basis for developing and evaluating TE capabilities. It was replaced by RFC 9522.

eli5.summary: Traffic engineering is steering network traffic so roads do not jam. This explains the main ideas. It has been replaced by RFC 9522.

subtitle: A framework for measuring, modeling and steering traffic so IP networks use their capacity well and avoid congestion.

tldr.problem: Operators of large IP networks need to keep performance good and avoid congestion, but shortest-path routing alone gives them little control over where traffic goes.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines traffic engineering as measuring, modeling and controlling traffic, lays out a repeating four-phase process, classifies TE systems, and recommends capabilities such as constraint-based routing and survivability.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational overview that gave later TE work a common vocabulary. It has since been obsoleted by RFC 9522 and updated by RFC 5462.

facts.value: Intra-domain TE, with an inter-domain overview

today: RFC 3272 is Informational and has been obsoleted by RFC 9522, so new readers should start there. It was also updated by RFC 5462.

sections.title: What Traffic Engineering Is
sections.content:
RFC 3272 describes the principles of Internet traffic engineering (TE). It defines TE as the part of network engineering that deals with performance evaluation and performance optimization of operational IP networks: the measurement, characterization, modeling and control of Internet traffic.

The goals are to meet traffic-oriented performance needs such as delay, delay variation, packet loss and throughput, while using network resources economically and reliably. The RFC points out that what end users see is what finally matters, so operators must be careful to optimize the right measures. Optimizing the wrong ones can help locally and hurt the network as a whole.

The document focuses on traffic engineering inside one autonomous system and gives a short overview of the inter-domain case. It pays more attention to TE with MPLS than to tuning IGP metrics. The text is for service providers and for vendors building TE tools. It is Informational and does not define a protocol.
sections.eli5: It is a guide for people who run big networks. It says how to watch the traffic, spot trouble early, and move things around so everybody's messages get through quickly.

sections.title: Congestion and How to Fight It
sections.content:
A network resource is congested when packets arrive faster than the resource can send them out over some interval. Congestion raises delay and delay variation, causes packet loss, and makes service less predictable. The RFC calls combating congestion at a reasonable cost a major objective of TE.

It sorts congestion management in three ways. By time scale: long (capacity planning, weeks to months or years), medium (minutes to days, such as adjusting IGP or BGP parameters or setting up explicit MPLS paths) and short (packet-level mechanisms, such as Random Early Detection queue management). By timing: reactive schemes respond to existing congestion, preventive ones act on predictions. By side: supply side schemes add or redistribute capacity, demand side schemes regulate the offered load.

The RFC concentrates on solutions that the network and its operators provide, rather than on adaptation in end systems.
sections.eli5: A traffic jam happens when more cars arrive than the road can carry. You can build a wider road, send cars down other streets, or let fewer cars in. Networks have the same three choices.

sections.title: The Traffic Engineering Process
sections.content:
The RFC describes an iterative process model with four phases that repeat continually. First, define the control policies that govern the network, based on factors such as the business model, cost structure and optimization criteria. Second, acquire measurement data from the operational network (or use synthetic workloads when real data is missing). Third, analyze the network state and characterize the workload, looking for bottlenecks and problems such as single points of failure. Fourth, optimize: pick and apply actions such as adding capacity, adjusting IGP metrics or BGP attributes, or tuning traffic management parameters.

Three subsystems carry this out: measurement, modeling and analysis (including simulation), and optimization. The RFC stresses that measurement is the only way to conclusively learn the operational state of a network, and that real-time optimization and longer-term network planning complement each other. Stability is a recurring concern when optimizing in real time.
sections.eli5: Make a plan, count the cars, figure out where the jams are, fix them, and then start again. You never really finish, because traffic keeps changing.

sections.title: Where the Ideas Came From
sections.content:
Section 4 reviews earlier approaches. Telephone networks moved from static hierarchical routing to dynamic routing: time-dependent, state-dependent and event-dependent. The text says dynamic routing typically cut overall loss probability by 10 to 20 percent compared with static hierarchical routing.

In packet networks, early ARPANET adaptive routing used delay tables, but dynamic link metrics tended to create traffic magnets that shifted congestion from place to place and caused oscillation. Static link metrics in IP routing ignored traffic and capacity, so some links congested while others stayed light. The RFC lists this inadequacy of legacy interior routing as one reason for interest in path-oriented technology with explicit and constraint-based routing, such as MPLS.

It also reviews the overlay model (IP over ATM or frame relay), Integrated Services, Differentiated Services, MPLS and other IETF and ITU work.
sections.eli5: Phone companies and the early internet both learned the hard way that fixed routes jam up and that rerouting too eagerly makes the jams just move around.

sections.title: A Taxonomy of TE Systems
sections.content:
The RFC classifies TE systems by style. Time-dependent TE pre-programs routing from historical patterns such as time of day. State-dependent TE adapts to the current network state. Event-dependent TE uses learning from events such as blocked setups and does not need to flood available-link-bandwidth information.

The other axes are offline versus online computation, centralized versus distributed control, local versus global state information, prescriptive (recommends actions) versus descriptive (only characterizes), open-loop versus closed-loop control, and tactical (fix a specific problem) versus strategic (systematic, long-term). The RFC notes that centralized control may produce better solutions but can be a single point of failure and may act on stale information, and it makes no recommendation between centralized and distributed schemes.
sections.eli5: You can plan the roads ahead of time or react as jams appear. One boss can direct everyone, or each driver can choose alone. This section just names all those choices.

sections.title: Recommendations
sections.content:
Section 6 gives high-level recommendations. Non-functional ones include usability, automation, scalability, stability, flexibility, visibility, simplicity, interoperability and security. On stability, the RFC strongly recommends that tradeoffs between responsiveness and stability be made in favor of stability, especially in public IP backbones.

For routing, it lists the limits of plain shortest-path IGPs: they cannot share load across paths of different cost, equal-cost multipath cannot set configurable ratios, and changing IGP metrics has network-wide effects. It recommends constraint-based routing, which computes routes subject to constraints such as bandwidth, hop count, delay and policy, and works best with explicit-routing technologies such as MPLS. It also covers traffic mapping (take care to keep packets of a micro-flow in order across parallel paths), measurement, multi-layer survivability (link, node, path and segment protection for MPLS), Diffserv environments and network controllability.

For inter-domain TE, the RFC says BGP attributes can influence exit points, that the outbound exit is controllable while inbound entry typically is not, and that BGP-based TE is usually applied by trial and error. Its Security Considerations section says only that the document introduces no new security issues.
sections.eli5: The advice is: keep things steady rather than twitchy, measure everything, give yourself ways to send some traffic down a different road, and have a backup route ready.

viz.caption: SEVEN WAYS TO CLASSIFY TE SYSTEMS (RFC 3272, SECTION 5)

items.title: Offline / Online
items.text: Whether plans are computed outside or inside the network.

items.title: Local / Global
items.text: How much network state is needed.

items.title: Prescriptive / Descriptive
items.text: Recommend actions or only describe state.

items.title: Open / Closed loop
items.text: Whether feedback from the network is used.

items.title: Tactical / Strategic
items.text: Ad hoc fixes or systematic planning.
